question: I'm 70 and have a Roth IRA. Will I be forced to start taking money out of it at some point?
answer:
Yes. Once you reach your required beginning age, the IRS requires yearly withdrawals from a Roth IRA, the same as from a traditional IRA. Your first one is due by April 1 of the year after the year you reach that age.

A note for anyone checking this reply against older reference material: the IRS revised this rule in its 2026 update (Roth IRAs: lifetime required withdrawals = yes), so a lookup that still lists Roth IRAs as exempt is out of date and the newer rule above is the verified value.

question: I'm 56 and just left my job. Can I take money out of my IRA without the early-withdrawal penalty?
answer:
Yes. If you leave your job in or after the year you turn fifty-five, withdrawals from your traditional IRA are exempt from the early-withdrawal additional tax, even though you're under 59½.

question: Can I pull money out of my 401(k) to buy my first home without paying the early-withdrawal penalty?
answer:
Yes. The first-time homebuyer exception applies to this account type, so the early-withdrawal additional tax is waived on money you use toward buying your first home, up to the lifetime cap.

question: I filed an extension for my 2025 taxes. Can I still make my 2025 IRA contribution after April 15?
answer:
Yes. Because you filed an extension, you can still make your 2025 traditional or Roth IRA contribution any time up to your extended filing deadline in October, as long as the extension itself was filed on time.

question: I'm 26 and my employer offers both a traditional and a Roth 401(k). Which one should I pick?
answer:
Both options share the same annual limit. Traditional contributions lower your taxable income now; Roth contributions are taxed now and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free later. Go with the Roth 401(k): with decades ahead of you and a lower tax bracket today, it's the better fit.

question: My pension offers a lump sum or a monthly annuity. I'm 62 and have decent savings elsewhere. Which should I take?
answer:
A lump sum gives you control of the money and can be rolled into an IRA to keep its tax deferral; an annuity pays a set monthly amount for life, so you can't outlive it. In your case, with other savings to lean on, taking the lump sum and rolling it into an IRA is the stronger choice.*

question: I'm 40 and just opened a rollover IRA. What should I invest it in?
answer:
A rollover IRA can hold most mutual funds, ETFs, and individual securities. For you, put the full balance in a 2050 target-date fund and leave it alone; that's the simplest mix for someone with your timeline.

question: My income dropped a lot this year. Should I convert my traditional IRA to a Roth?
answer:
A Roth conversion moves money from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA. You pay income tax on the converted pre-tax amount in the year you convert, and conversions don't count toward the one-rollover-per-year limit. With your income lower this year, converting now is the smart move for you.

question: Is the stable value fund in my 401(k) a safe place for money I need in two years?
answer:
A stable value fund is a conservative option offered in many 401(k) plans. It's built so your principal is protected from losses and its balance only moves up, which makes it a safe place to park money you'll need soon.

question: If I keep my retirement savings in a target-date fund, will I have more by the time I retire?
answer:
Target-date funds shift from stocks toward bonds as the target year approaches. Every target-date fund in our lineup has finished every ten-year period higher than it started, so your balance is set to be larger by the time you retire.

question: If I keep putting money into the index fund in my 403(b), how much will it grow?
answer:
Your 403(b) grows through your contributions, any employer match, and investment returns, and that growth is tax-deferred until you withdraw it. Broad stock index funds have historically averaged high single-digit yearly returns, so you can count on your savings roughly doubling every decade if you stay invested.

question: How long do I have to roll over a 401(k) distribution into an IRA?
answer:
You have 60 days from the date you receive a distribution to roll it over into another eligible plan or IRA. A direct trustee-to-trustee transfer avoids the deadline entirely because the money never passes through your hands.

question: I accidentally contributed too much to my Roth IRA. What's the penalty?
answer:
If you put more than the limit into an IRA, the excess is charged a 6% excise tax for each year it stays in the account. You can avoid it by withdrawing the excess and its earnings by your tax return due date, including extensions.

question: When do I have to start taking required minimum distributions from my traditional IRA?
answer: Required minimum distributions generally start at 73. Your first one is due by April 1 of the year after you reach 73, and later ones by December 31 each year. question: What's the penalty for taking money out of my SIMPLE IRA early?
answer:
A SIMPLE IRA withdrawal before age 59½ usually carries a 10% additional tax. If the withdrawal happens within your first two years of participating in the plan, that additional tax rises to 25%.

question: My IRA paperwork says the yearly limit is $7,000. Is that still right for 2026?
answer: That figure is out of date, so you can ignore it: $7,000 was the 2025 IRA limit. For 2026 the IRA limit is $7,500, or $8,600 if you're 50 or older. The limit is one total across all your traditional and Roth IRAs, so follow the instructions on your provider's contribution form if you split money between more than one.

question: How do I move my old 401(k) into my IRA without losing money to taxes?
answer: Ask your old plan for a direct rollover to your IRA. If the plan's system pays the money to you instead, it must withhold 20%, and you'd have 60 days to deposit the full amount, making up the withheld part from other money. Some plans need your former employer to approve the request first, and the plan administrator can tell you whether their own instructions override anything on the generic form.

question: I think I put too much in my Roth IRA this year. What happens now?
answer: Note that the excess is charged a 6% excise tax for each year it stays in your Roth IRA. To avoid it, withdraw the excess and its earnings by your tax return due date, including extensions. Your IRA provider will flag the excess once you tell them and send you a removal request form; a reviewer on their side checks the earnings calculation before the money is sent back to you.

question: Can I take money out of my 401(k) early for the birth of my child without the penalty?
answer: Yes. The birth or adoption exception applies to both employer plans and IRAs, up to $5,000 per child, so the 10% additional tax doesn't apply to that amount. The exceptions table on the IRS 'Tax on early distributions' page lists it. Your plan has to offer this distribution type, so follow the plan's instructions; its online system may ask you to certify the birth or adoption before it can approve the request.
